note: Landing a Dorian solo on the notes of the chord playing: any triad note on a solo-over, then only the 3rds, then free phrases over the full backing track across three framed positions. The chords are tokens counted the long way once and every note a degree token, the key is moves (any key) and named only as {{=key}}, each block has one extra line, and the {{?key}} line says what stays the same.

exercise.title: Triad notes in a Dorian solo
exercise.why: The triads of the 1st and 4th chords are made of notes of the Dorian scale, so their notes are the places a solo over those two chords can land.

cells.text:
The backing track switches between two chords of {{=key}} Dorian. {{chord:i7}} is the 1st chord of the key, built on {{1}}. {{chord:IV7}} is the 4th chord, built on {{4}}.
Press Play below to start the backing track. Improvise in {{=key}} Dorian and end each phrase on a ringed note: the ringed notes are the triad of the chord playing.
If a phrase ends between two ringed notes, move its last note one step up or down to the nearer one.

Press Play below to start the backing track again. Now the ringed note is the 3rd of each chord: {{b3}} over {{chord:i7}} and {{6}} over {{chord:IV7}}. Aim every phrase at it.
The 3rd of {{chord:IV7}} is also the 6th of the Dorian scale, the note that sets the mode apart, so landing on it says both the chord and the mode.

Press Play below to start the backing track with drums, bass and keys. Under it are positions 1, 2 and 3 of the {{=key}} Dorian scale. Open a phrase with a few notes of the triad of the chord playing, carry on with the scale, and end on a note of that triad.
Practice until you hear which chord is playing without looking at the boxes.
{{?key}}In another key the positions sit on other frets, and the 3rd of {{chord:IV7}} is still {{6}}.
